name: Haloperidol
route_note: Oral tablets or solution; IM lactate for acute agitation; monthly IM decanoate depot; IV use is off-label in the US.

discovery.by: Paul Janssen and colleagues (Janssen Pharmaceutica, Beerse)
discovery.note: Synthesised in February 1958 during work on pethidine analogues; it showed potent amphetamine-antagonising, chlorpromazine-like activity.

tagline: High-potency butyrophenone antipsychotic used for psychosis, delirium and agitation
summary: Haloperidol is a high-potency first-generation antipsychotic discovered by Paul Janssen in 1958. It is used for schizophrenia, acute agitation, delirium, Tourette syndrome and nausea in palliative care, and is available as a long-acting depot injection.
mechanism: Haloperidol is a potent and relatively selective dopamine D2 receptor antagonist, with much less histamine, muscarinic and adrenergic blockade than chlorpromazine. This produces strong antipsychotic and antiemetic effects with little sedation or hypotension.
High D2 occupancy in the striatum results in a high rate of extrapyramidal side effects, including acute dystonia, parkinsonism and akathisia.
uses: Nausea and vomiting in palliative care

history.title: Launch
history.detail: Haloperidol is introduced in Belgium and soon across Europe.

history.title: Decanoate
history.detail: The long-acting decanoate depot is approved in the US.

history.title: IV warning
history.detail: The FDA warns of QT prolongation and torsade de pointes, especially with IV use or high doses.

history.title: Dementia warning
history.detail: The boxed warning on mortality in elderly patients with dementia is extended to typical antipsychotics.

pk.half_life: 14–37 hours oral; about 3 weeks for decanoate
pk.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation, reduction and CYP3A4/2D6 oxidation

serious: QT prolongation and torsade de pointes
safety.boxed_warning: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; not approved for this use.

facts: Haloperidol is the prototype butyrophenone; the same chemical programme led Janssen to fentanyl and droperidol.
